paragraphs.text: CHAPTERS OF THE FIRST BOOK.
I. That the Holy Spirit is to be understood wholly and plainly from the head of the faith, that is, from the Creed.
II. That we ought not to believe in the Church as we believe in the Holy Spirit, but to believe the catholic Church, with the preposition "in" removed.
III. That Christ was not begotten but created by the Holy Spirit, inasmuch as the Spirit is God.
IV. On establishing the unity by the testimonies of the prophets.
V. On the Trinity, and that even the liberal disciplines recognized three persons.
VI. When the Son is called the face of the Father, he is acknowledged to be coeternal with the Father.
VII. That the Spirit of the Father is the Holy Spirit himself.
VIII. On the finger of God.
IX. That it does not detract from the deity of the Holy Spirit that he appears to be neither unbegotten nor begotten.
X. That the Holy Spirit is the bestower of the perfect gifts.
XI. The assertion of the Trinity is repeated from the Acts of the Apostles, where Christ is also declared, against the Novatians, to have been sent to grant repentance.
XII. That it belongs to God alone to sanctify the creature.
XIII. That the Holy Spirit is not confined to a place.
THAT THE HOLY SPIRIT IS TO BE UNDERSTOOD WHOLLY AND PLAINLY FROM THE HEAD OF THE FAITH, THAT IS, FROM THE CREED.

The catholic faith has been spread throughout the whole world by the patriarchs and prophets and the dispensers of grace, at the prompting of the Holy Spirit. The care and perfection of the apostles, which had spread this faith abroad through the sacred pages, likewise gathered it with wonderful brevity into the saving formula of the Creed. It arranged, as it were, scattered kinds of remedies into a single body, and as though from countless spices it compounded a precious ointment, whose scent has filled all the ends of the earth with the power of its spiritual fragrance, so that the strength of the truth might appear in the very assent of the whole world.

And since we must repeat the first elements of the Christian tradition to those who are in error, as to little children and the ignorant: in this perfect Creed both the unity and the Trinity are plainly disclosed, when the confession, repeated three times, renders one obedience of faith to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. In these words, too, the sacred number of the three hundred and eighteen bishops condemned the rising error of Arius and Macedonius, [saying]: I believe in God the Father, I believe in his only Son our Lord, I believe also in the Holy Spirit. For even if the weakness of a few out of that number swerved from this, it did not undo the mystery of the number as a whole. We have called it a sacred number because, in Greek numerals or reckoning, three hundred represents the sign of the cross, and eighteen the adorable name of Jesus. In this number and mystery, then, in which holy Abraham also triumphed over countless nations, the piety of the elders confounded the enemy of the faith under the single proclamation of Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Hence it must also be understood that those who blaspheme against the Holy Spirit, under eternal damnation, were either baptized without the complete Creed, or else lied to themselves in the very Creed and at the very font before which every person, renouncing the devil, confesses: I believe also in the Holy Spirit.

I believe, I say, also in the Holy Spirit. Let us recognize the special privilege of this very word. You may believe any man you please, but know that believing in someone you owe to the divine Majesty alone. Indeed, it is one thing to believe God, and another to believe in God. Even the devil is said to believe that God exists, according to the apostle: for the demons also believe and tremble. But no one is shown to believe in God unless he has hoped in him with devotion. To believe in God, then, is to seek him faithfully and to pass over into him with all one's love. So to say "I believe in him" is to say: I confess him, I worship him, I adore him, I hand over and pour out my whole self into his right and dominion. In the reverence of this profession is contained all the homage owed to the divine name.
II. THAT WE OUGHT NOT TO BELIEVE IN THE CHURCH AS WE BELIEVE IN THE HOLY SPIRIT, BUT TO BELIEVE THE CATHOLIC CHURCH, WITH THE PREPOSITION "IN" REMOVED.

But you object and say that God cannot at once be proved by the phrase in which we say "I believe also in the Holy Spirit," because there follows: "I believe in the holy catholic Church." First, I do not know how Macedonius dares to name the catholic Church at all, he who, shut out from the catholic Church as an exile [?] from salvation, has become one of those of whom it is said: The wicked walk round about. So you say: "I believe in the holy catholic Church." Why do you try, by slipping in a tiny syllable, namely "in," to weave in so vast a darkness? We believe the Church as the mother of our regeneration; we do not believe in the Church as in the author of our salvation. For since the whole Church confesses this of the Holy Spirit, can the Church also believe in itself? Therefore, since the teaching of the fathers we have mentioned, celebrated throughout the whole world, confirms that belief "in" is owed specifically to the Trinity alone, either remove this syllable from the name of the Church, or else establish from the Scriptures, by an explicit statement, that you believe in the Church: teach it by testimonies, prove it by the divine oracles, setting aside the presumption of your own words.

Let us by all means take what is to be believed from the sacred books, from whose fountain the whole sequence of the Creed itself is derived and stands. Whoever believes in the Church believes in a human being. For man did not come from the Church; rather, the Church began to exist from man. Withdraw, then, from this blasphemous notion that you ought to believe in any human creature, since one must not believe in an angel or an archangel at all. For the articles that follow the name of the Holy Spirit in the Creed refer back, with the preposition "in" removed, to the governing clause of the Creed, so that we believe the holy Church, the communion of saints, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the flesh and eternal life in God; that is, we confess that these things have been ordained by God and stand firm in God. For the ignorance of some has snatched this preposition from the neighboring clause close by, dragged it into the one that follows, and thoughtlessly added it where it is superfluous. But in none of the canonical writings, on which the text of the Creed depends, do we find that we ought to believe in the Church as we believe in the Holy Spirit and the Son. And therefore, since every creature is excluded from this honor, the Holy Spirit, in whom we are commanded to believe, is God. This expression the voice of the Lord and Saviour assigns specifically to the Godhead, saying: Believe in God, and believe in me; and again: Whoever believes in me does not believe in me, but in him who sent me.
III. THAT CHRIST WAS NOT BEGOTTEN BUT CREATED BY THE HOLY SPIRIT, INASMUCH AS THE SPIRIT IS GOD.

Now since the catholic Church confesses "conceived by the Holy Spirit," the Macedonians must be asked at this point whether they consider the Holy Spirit the creator or the father of the Redeemer. If perhaps they answer "father," then, since at the very beginning of the Creed they have already said "I believe in God the Father almighty," they will be confusedly confessing that he has two fathers. But if they declare him creator, as the truth has it, they will be compelled, if only by necessity, to proclaim with us that he is Lord of the universe. And so he speaks through the prophet Isaiah, as through his own trumpet and from his own temple, foreshadowing the two substances in Christ: Drop down dew from above, you heavens, and let the clouds rain down the Just One; let the earth be opened and bud forth the Saviour; I the Lord have created him. For the man taken from Mary was the work of the Holy Spirit, not a portion of him; he was not begotten by him, but created. He was conceived by power, not by substance; by operation, not by participation; by might, not by generation.
IV. ON ESTABLISHING THE UNITY BY THE TESTIMONIES OF THE PROPHETS.

The catholic faith venerates a threefold majesty under the confession of one Godhead [receive the one Godhead from the sacred books]: Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God; and: You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone; and again: I am the Lord, and there is no God besides me; and in the Psalms: You who work wonders, you alone are God; likewise: You alone are the Most High over all the earth. Through Isaiah also: God of Israel, who sit above the cherubim, you alone are God of all the kingdoms of the earth; likewise: I am the Lord, I am the first and the last; likewise: I am the Lord, that is my name; my glory I will not give to another. And so that you may know that this testimony, namely "the first and the last," refers to Christ, he said of himself in another place: I am the beginning, who also speak to you; likewise: Before me there was no God, and after me there shall be none. I am the Lord, and apart from me there is no saviour, which applies especially to Christ, the Saviour of the human race; likewise: Thus says the Lord, your redeemer, who formed you from the womb: I am the Lord who makes all things, who stretches out the heavens, who alone establishes the earth, and no one is with me. This refers properly to Jesus, the maker and redeemer, of whom the evangelist records: All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made; likewise: There is no God besides me, and there is no saviour apart from me; likewise: I am the first and I am the last; my hand also laid the foundation of the earth, and my right hand measured out the heavens, just as Jesus Christ plainly declares of himself in another place, saying: I [am] the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end. The Holy Spirit too is included in these testimonies, and in them the unity of the divine substance must be confessed with regard to the Holy Spirit in such a way that we believe that there is in them also a distinct property of persons and an undivided plurality.
V. ON THE TRINITY, AND THAT EVEN THE LIBERAL DISCIPLINES RECOGNIZED THREE PERSONS.

So, having shown one Godhead from the words of God, let us now teach three in the one Godhead: three names, not three kingdoms; three designations, but not three powers; three essences or subsistences, but not three substances. It is clear that even worldly wisdom has understood that the whole multitude of all the ages is enclosed within the scheme of three persons. What are these three? Namely: I, you, he. So, as we have said, even the liberal studies, by instruction borrowed from spiritual teaching, perceived that there are only three persons in the nature of things; and it was evident to them that a second person does not suffice for completeness, nor can a third be exceeded. For fullness, which tends toward the number three, shows that a pair is only half complete, while perfection, consummated in three, rejects a fourth. Having passed over these matters with a brief mention, let us rather establish from the sacred testimonies that the Trinity subsists in unity.

But you say: Why do you bring before me the words "unity" and "trinity," which you do not find in the canonical reading? No wonder that one who does not deserve to enter the inner chambers of salvation is terrified and shrinks back even from the door of truth. For what could be so close, so natural, so fitting as that, in the catholic definitions of the fathers, "unity" should be named from "one" and "trinity" from "three"? Words that depend on what precedes them are not to be examined in isolation, nor does it follow that words should be judged foreign which are born of "one" and "three," that is, from the proper sense of a plain origin. Notice that neither of these terms is presumptuous; both are derived. These are terms that antiquity found from the time of the primitive Church, that authority put forward, and that long ages have confirmed.
VI. WHEN THE SON IS CALLED THE FACE OF THE FATHER, HE IS ACKNOWLEDGED TO BE COETERNAL WITH THE FATHER.

Receive the Trinity from the sacred books: In the beginning God made heaven and earth, and the Spirit of God moved over the waters. The Father is the author, the Son the coeternal beginning, the Holy Spirit the one poured over the waters. So the exalted one who rules was borne over the waters, even then, I believe, prefiguring the gifts of baptism. In the making of man, too, the threefold repetition of the Godhead shows that this is the work not of one person but of three. For we read: And God said: Let us make man in our image and likeness. Notice that the statement is single in its subject and manifold in its answer. And God said: Let us make man. What does this mean but that the substance of the unity speaks and the power of the Trinity acts? Observe how the name of God is pronounced three times in the creation of man. For so we have it in Genesis: And God said: Let us make man; and again: God created man; and a third time: God blessed him. God said, God made, God blessed. The one Godhead is repeated three times because of the three persons. In this passage understand clearly the mystery of the unity as well. See, the image and likeness of God is given to each human being by three, and yet it is recognized to be one. God said: Let us make. Pay careful attention: one speaks, and not one makes; and when he again mingles singular with plural, and does not say "in our images and likenesses," nor indeed "in my image and likeness," he commends the unity by the singular and the Trinity by the plural. So in saying "Let us make... in our," the number of persons is set forth; but in saying in the singular "in the image and likeness," the undivided Godhead is gathered into one substance.

When God appeared to Abraham at the door of his tent, and three wondrously presented themselves to his eyes in place of one, he, aware of the majesty, worshipped one in three. In the Psalms too the unity is plainly designated with its persons: Do not cast me away, he says, from your face, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me. See, the prophet, praying to the Father, dreads offending the Holy Spirit no less than the Father and the Son. Do not cast me away, he says, from your face. Just as the Son is understood to be the image of the Father, so too he is understood to be the face of the Father. And so we read: Philip, whoever sees me sees the Father also; likewise: Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your face? Notice, unbeliever, the mystery of the Trinity in a perfect confession. The prophet speaks to the Father, confesses the Son as the face of the Father, and also bears witness to the Holy Spirit diffused through all things. Concerning the Son, the Lord also says to Moses: My face shall go before you. This name, "face," pertains both to the unity of substance and to the coeternity of majesty. And as for their thinking him lesser because he was born: what does it mean for God to be born of God, if not to have come forth from God by nature? But you say: If he is from him, he is younger than he. Look: the arm springs from the body and the face from its head, yet it is agreed that the face is not younger than its head, nor the arm later than its body. If, then, any head was ever older than its face, then go ahead and claim that the Father is older than his image, which consists in the perfect likeness and equality of Christ. So the Son can no more be distinguished from the Father in power or in time than a face can be separated from its head or be found in any way younger than its head.
VII. THAT THE SPIRIT OF THE FATHER IS THE HOLY SPIRIT HIMSELF.

But you say: Show me that the Holy Spirit subsists in his own essence. Wherever or whenever I read "the Spirit of the Father" or "my Spirit" or "the Spirit of God," I see, you say, that it is to be referred not to the person of the Holy Spirit but to that of the Father. First of all, they heap up the blasphemy of their impiety here, when they say that the Holy Spirit of God is to be believed either a creature or else the Father himself. Rightly does the one who does not confess the Holy Spirit tumble, with his mind in confusion, even into insulting the Father. Surely, if the Spirit is a thing made, he cannot belong to the Father's substance. But if you think he is the Father's power, how do you presume to degrade him to the insult of being a thing made? We, however, will show by clear testimonies that "the Spirit of God" is said not of the Father but properly of the Holy Spirit.

We read in Isaiah that the Spirit of the Lord descended upon the Lord Jesus: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and godliness. Of this Spirit of the Lord, who came down upon the Saviour in a sacred descent, the Son says through Isaiah: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; and the evangelist Matthew says: Behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending upon him like a dove. And that this Spirit of God, whom the Saviour received at his baptism, is plainly the Holy Spirit, Luke the evangelist has fully taught, saying: Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan. We read in the prophet Joel: In those days I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh. It is clear that his words "of my Spirit" were said of the Holy Spirit, because when the Holy Spirit came down upon the apostles on the sacred feast of Pentecost, the apostle Peter then took up this testimony from the prophet.

Moreover, the Gospels have taught, in different words but with harmonious truth, that the Spirit of the Father is the Holy Spirit himself. For while Matthew said: For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you, Mark openly explained that this Spirit of the Father is the Holy Spirit, saying: Whatever is given you in that hour, speak that; for it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit. And Luke likewise showed that this Spirit of God is the Holy Spirit, saying: Do not be anxious about how or what you are to say; for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that hour what you ought to say. In accordance with these passages, then, whenever you read "the Spirit of the Father" or "the Spirit of God," you must lay aside your error and confess that it is to be referred specifically to the Holy Spirit. Likewise Isaiah too counts the Holy Spirit as one in the glory of the Trinity when he says: I saw the Lord sitting on a lofty throne, and the Seraphim stood and cried one to another: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth. And further on he says: And I heard the voice of the Lord saying: Go and say to this people: Hearing you will hear and not understand, and seeing you will see and not see. Who this Lord of Sabaoth was, who was seen by the prophet in an assumed form and who spoke in the prophet, Paul shows in the Acts of the Apostles, saying: Well did the Holy Spirit speak through the prophet Isaiah to our fathers: Hearing you will hear and not understand, and seeing you will see and not see.

Let us at least believe Paul, the most renowned herald of the truth, that the Holy Spirit was that Lord of hosts whom Isaiah saw and who spoke through Isaiah. But since "holy, holy, holy" rings out in a threefold repetition, let us see whether this honor looks to the whole Trinity. When Isaiah says "I saw the Lord of Sabaoth," the Jews recognize him as proclaiming the Father. The evangelist John is shown openly to declare the Son, saying: For this reason they could not believe in Jesus, because Isaiah said: He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart. Isaiah said these things when he saw the glory of the Son of God and spoke of him. And as for the same Isaiah's words: And I heard the voice of the Lord saying: Go and say to this people: Seeing you will see and not see, the apostle Paul, as we have said, confirms that this Lord is the Holy Spirit. You see, then, that this cry, "holy, holy, holy," celebrates the whole Trinity together; and just as there is no dissimilarity and no difference among these three words, so in the power of the Trinity there can be no distance.
VIII. ON THE FINGER OF GOD.

But you say: "It is plainly recognized that the Holy Spirit is lesser from the fact that he is called the finger of God." It is not so. When you hear it said of the Holy Spirit, "If I cast out demons by the finger of God," understand that what is shown is not a lessening of glory but the unity of substance; not a difference in honor but harmony in work. What then? Because the Holy Spirit is sometimes called the finger (of God), is he therefore believed to be less than the Son and the Father? Flee the error of this notion, and consider that this term "finger" sometimes includes both the Father and the Son. Let us remember that it is not one finger that is spoken of when we read: "For I will see your heavens, the works of your fingers." But you say that in "fingers" only the Son and the Holy Spirit are signified, as a kind of pair. To keep you from trying to assert this of two persons, in another place Isaiah speaks of the Trinity by the number of exactly three fingers, saying: "Who has weighed the mass of the earth with three fingers?" What could be plainer, what clearer, about the unity of the Trinity? Has he not here, in three fingers, weighed the equality of one power on a kind of mystic scale? Therefore, as has been said, now that you have been taught about their partnership in work, do not doubt the equality of their power. So in saying, "Who has weighed the mass of the earth with three fingers?" he meant here to speak specifically of their cooperation in power and their unity of substance, which is shown to be one and the same in the three fingers.

Nonetheless, notice in the prophet Isaiah the proper person of the Holy Spirit within the distinction of the Trinity, where the Son, speaking of himself, "I am the first and I am the last," then added: "And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit." God the Father is one in person, and the Spirit of God the Father is another. So when we read that the Son is sent by the Father and the Holy Spirit, it is plainly disclosed, under the names of three persons, that the Holy Spirit subsists in himself. In the same way, in another place, the same prophet distinguishes the being of the Trinity: "Behold my servant, I will uphold him, my beloved, in whom my soul is well pleased; I have put my Spirit upon him." The Father calls the Son his beloved servant, upon whom he has put his Spirit, to which Jesus Christ testifies with his own voice: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me." And so that the gospel might be made known to the Gentiles too, he says: "Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit," where under three persons he declares one work and one name, an undivided majesty. We have, as it is told according to Luke: "And when Jesus had been baptized, heaven was opened, and the Holy Spirit descended in bodily form like a dove, and a voice came from heaven: You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased." So the Son is made known in the body, the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove, the Father in the voice. But here we must understand the dove as a passing form, not an abiding substance.
IX. THAT IT IS NO OBSTACLE TO THE DEITY OF THE HOLY SPIRIT THAT HE IS SAID TO BE NEITHER UNBEGOTTEN NOR BEGOTTEN.

But amid all this, since we show the proper person of the Holy Spirit and confess the Father as unbegotten, and acknowledge the Son as only-begotten, you ask me whether the Holy Spirit should be confessed as unbegotten, or begotten, or something else. The holy Scriptures speak of the power and deity of the Holy Spirit, but whether he should be called begotten or unbegotten they do not say. See what darkness unbelief makes for itself. You do not want to know what God did not wish to be unknown, and you want to know what he did not command to be inquired into. He did not say "begotten," so that you would not believe him to be the Son; he did not say "unbegotten," so that you would not think him to be the Father. Rather, to distinguish his being, Scripture testified that he proceeds from the Father, as we read: "the Paraclete, who proceeds from the Father." This being so, at least recognize from it that the Holy Spirit has his own person. The difference of name proves that there is a third besides the two; the unity of majesty shows that he who proceeds from God is not third in order or rank. For he who comes forth from the inmost being of God is proved to be not a creature of God but the substance of God. Do not pry into how he is God when it is clear that he is God. Here the reasoning is hidden; the truth is not hidden. Why ask how he is the companion and equal of the king, when he is known to be of royal honor and royal lineage? Inquiry about the name is superfluous where there is no doubt about his exaltedness. So, because the Holy Spirit proceeds from both, Scripture says, "But whoever does not have the Spirit of the Lord does not belong to him," and in another place, "He breathed on them and said: Receive the Holy Spirit."

You ask whether he is unbegotten or begotten. The sacred oracles have uttered nothing about this, and it is wrong to break in upon the divine silence. What God did not think fit to disclose in his Scriptures, he did not want you to ask about or know out of needless curiosity. He judged that what concerns your salvation is what ought to reach your understanding. Let us consult the holy oracles about what we should believe concerning the Holy Spirit. For would you dare to say even this, that the Son is begotten, if you had not learned it from the heavenly testimony of the Scriptures? Or would you presume to assert that Christ the Lord was born of the Virgin, or begotten of the Father, who is coeval and coeternal with him, if you had not taken it from reading, if you had not asked the divine words about God? And so, to learn how you ought to think about the Holy Spirit, you must return to the apostles and the Gospels, with whom and in whom you do not doubt that God has spoken.

So, to return to your pointless question: does the glory or substance of the Holy Spirit depend on whether he is shown to be unbegotten or begotten? It takes nothing from the Son that we do not read that he is unbegotten, nor from the Father that he is not held to be begotten. In terms like these there is a distinction of naming, not a difference of power or majesty. "Begotten" and "unbegotten" mark a difference of person, not of nature. So when you have said or heard about "begotten" and "unbegotten" things that are useless, unnecessary, and fit only for cavilling, will you be content to stop there? Surely you will go on to ask whether he is God. But once you have learned from what is read that he is God, you will have nothing left to ask, because once you begin to know things that are solid and complete, you will have no need to inquire into things that are empty and hollow. Where, then, a sound reason is found to be useful and the fullness of truth is found, let a mind seeking salvation direct itself there.
X. THAT THE HOLY SPIRIT IS THE BESTOWER OF PERFECT GIFTS.

The very meaning of his name testifies that the Holy Spirit is the bestower of heavenly gifts and the dispenser of sanctification. His magnificence was made known even in the Old Testament. For there his grace was granted only to certain chosen ones, namely the patriarchs and prophets and the holy and elect, so that from the very perfection of the gifts I might understand the dignity of the giver. And so far as is very plainly found in the holy Scriptures, the Father does some things by himself, some particularly through the Son, and some through the Holy Spirit, though all within the prerogative of a common power. That we exist seems to be properly referred to the Father, in whom, as the apostle said, we live and move and have our being. That we are capable of reason, wisdom, and righteousness is particularly credited to him who is reason, wisdom, and righteousness, that is, to the Son. And that, once called, we are reborn, and once reborn are renewed, and once renewed are sanctified, is clearly ascribed by the divine oracles to the person of the Holy Spirit.

But the sacred pages speak of these things, distinguishing within the undivided Trinity, in such a way that, however much a difference of work appears in each, the unity of will remains in the three. Thus both Gentiles and catechumens share in the dispensation of the Father and the Son; but in the sanctification and outpouring of the Holy Spirit they do not readily share, unless they have already received baptism and been purified and made spiritual; and so too apostolic men and apostles, and those prepared with their whole spirit for martyrdom. And amid all this, will the impious still judge to be a creature him who, within the undivided Trinity, in ordering human salvation, is allotted all the more magnificent and more perfect gifts? But perhaps you will say: "Then the Holy Spirit is greater, since his works are greater and nobler." It is not so. For it is the Trinity's custom that to whichever person it entrusts the task of carrying out a matter, it credits the effect once accomplished; thus the work may perhaps be different, but the purpose is common. And if each has a particular deed, a common counsel remains in the three; and so, though they have distinct tasks in operation, they hold one agreement in its ordering.

After the Lord's ascension, the Holy Spirit is described as having descended to crown and complete his benefits. The Savior himself speaks of him in John's Gospel: "That Spirit of truth, whom the Father will send in my name." "The Father will send," he says, "in my name": plainly of the Trinity. Of what creature have we ever read or heard it said that it came into this world in the name of God? This one, then, of whom Christ the Lord God says, "Unless I go, the Paraclete will not come to you," is without doubt God, sent in God's place to confirm God's gifts. In these two sayings the person of the Holy Spirit too is fully declared within the distinction of the Trinity. So it is with good reason that this also is referred to his equality in divinity: that, like the Son, the Holy Spirit too is called Paraclete in the Scriptures. And how can we prove this? From the authority of the apostle John, when he says: "If any of us sins, we have a Paraclete with the Father, Jesus Christ, and he is the propitiation for our sins." One Greek word, "Paraclete," signifies both "advocate," which applies to the person of the Son, and "comforter," which belongs to the Holy Spirit. In John's Gospel we have: "And I," he says, "will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete." "Another Paraclete": that is, of like power, equal glory, and the same nature. "And another Paraclete": if you think the Holy Spirit is one of the creatures, it is unworthy that at his descent a creature should confirm the benefits the Creator conferred, and that, as though the Maker's power had been ineffective, the completion of an unfinished work should be reserved for a creature, however excellent.

So you revile the Holy Spirit with the reproach of being a creature, though the Son of God made himself equal to him by divine testimony from his own lips. "And another Paraclete": recognize here in a twofold sense both the distinction of person and the equality of substance. Here perhaps you will object: "Christ seems to have made himself equal, under the name of Paraclete, to the Holy Spirit, who is certainly the material of God's work and something made, because Jesus himself is shown to have been created from Mary." This argument is as weak as it is faithless. For if you think Christ was likened to the Paraclete according to his humanity, even this does not fit the truth. For he who was made a little lower than the angels and became one of us could not be compared with the first, heavenly, and, as you assert, more excellent creature. But if Christ said this according to the form of God, it is certain that what is made ought not to be compared with its Maker. So if a man makes himself equal to this more excellent creature, it is the pride of the lesser; if God does so, it is an insult to the greater. Since, then, this comparison cannot hold if he is in the condition of a creature, it remains that both be believed to be God and that equality of divinity be shared between them. For when the Savior says through John, "And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, whom this world cannot receive," he who can be given to the whole world is clearly the God of the world. Recognize here too the threefold Trinity. It is the Father who is named as the one to be asked, the Son who is understood as the one who will ask, the Holy Spirit who is promised as the one to be sent by the Father. Notice that the person of the Holy Spirit is not associated, as you assert, with creatures as his kin, but is joined to the Trinity in all its works and made equal to it in its powers.
XI. THAT THE AFFIRMATION OF THE TRINITY IS REPEATED IN THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES, WHERE CHRIST IS ALSO DECLARED, AGAINST THE NOVATIANS, TO HAVE BEEN SENT TO GRANT REPENTANCE.

In the Acts of the Apostles, Peter, speaking of the Lord Jesus, says: "Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this, which you see and hear." In "the right hand" the Son is indicated, in "God" the Father, and the Holy Spirit by his own proper name. And further on we read: "Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead, by him this man stands before you whole." See here too the distinction of the Trinity expressed. Peter, bearing the Holy Spirit within him, speaks of the Son dying in the flesh and the Father raising him. There, likewise, it is repeated in the apostles' words: "And now, Lord," they say, "look upon their threats," and: "They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke the word of God with boldness." Notice in this place too that the Holy Spirit is included in the Trinity. In the prayer the Father is addressed; in the word of God the Son is recognized; in the apostles' steadfastness the fire of the Holy Spirit is at work. "They were all filled with the Holy Spirit": it belongs to evident majesty to be able to pour itself into many at once by the subtlety of incorporeal divinity, and to remain whole without loss. Again, when the apostles had said of Jesus, "God exalted him with his right hand as Prince and Savior, to grant repentance to Israel for the forgiveness of sins," they said: "We are witnesses of these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to all who obey him." Understand here that, in the order of the Trinity, the Son is sent by the Father not only to preach repentance but to grant it, and that the Holy Spirit is poured into those who obey, to reward their obedience.

Stephen is filled with the Holy Spirit at the moment of his passion, and when the gates of righteousness are opened to him the Son is revealed at the right hand of the Father, as he himself, filled with the Holy Spirit, declares: "Behold, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God." See how he performed the service of his passion with the Trinity before his eyes. Peter addresses the centurion Cornelius, saying: "Jesus of Nazareth, how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit." God anointed him: that is, power filled him, blessing was poured into him, divinity pervaded him. "How God anointed him with the Holy Spirit": here three plainly appear, each with its own property: the gift, the giver, and the one gifted; the one anointing, the one anointed, and the ointment. So too the divine word says in another place: "God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness." In the humanity he took up, God is anointed and God anoints, and in the descent of the heavenly dove the power of the Father is recognized. It is not right to believe that this Holy Spirit, by whom Christ the Son of Man, already full as Son of God, is filled, is anything other than God. For if he were a creature, how could he pervade an incorporeal nature that pervades all things? For the Trinity can contain itself, as we have it: "I am in the Father and the Father in me," and again: "The Spirit searches even the depths of God," and also: "The Spirit, who proceeds from the Father." Unless this Holy Spirit were from the Father, and dwelt in him by nature, poured into the Father's inmost being, he could not proceed from the Father.

But you ask whether the Spirit proceeds from the Father always. Always with him, always from him, as heat from fire, he is brought forth without interruption, so that he knows how to go forth but does not know how to be separated. For if the procession of the Holy Spirit were not everlasting, his substance would seem to be bounded by place. If the incorporeal brightness, which is able to contain itself, does not pass into each other without being mingled, then the divinity will be confused [?]. For mingling destroys what is proper to the threefold being, whereas mutual indwelling shows a distinct being, which may be seen as a mean between the substance and the persons. To the substance belongs that it subsists; to the persons belongs that each subsists properly in itself. Paul addresses his disciples, saying: "I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God. Take heed to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you bishops, to rule the Church of God, which he purchased with his own blood." How clearly the whole Trinity is set out in its persons! He proclaims the counsel of God the Father, affirms that the bishops were ordained by the Holy Spirit, and shows that Christ, by whose blood the Church was purchased, is also God.

In Romans too the Trinity is set out with the proper names: "But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus Christ dwells in you, he who raised Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you." The Father raises, the Son is raised, and through the indwelling Spirit life is promised for the raising of mortal bodies. And next: "But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him." Since he says "the Spirit of God" and then "the Spirit of Christ," notice that here he designates the person of Christ by the name "God." Or if here by the name "God" he means the Father, whose Spirit he is, then see: the Holy Spirit is declared, through the unity of substance, to be the Spirit of both the Father and the Son; he is rightly recognized as proceeding from both; he is seen to have a distinct person within the bond of the Trinity; and whoever does not have the Holy Spirit is shown not to have Christ either. The Holy Spirit, therefore, is God, and to deny him is to deny Christ as well; and since Christ said, "No one comes to the Father except through me," whoever is empty of the Holy Spirit is not Christ's and has lost the way by which one reaches the Father.
XII. THAT IT IS PROPER TO GOD TO SANCTIFY THE CREATURE.

First Corinthians: "And such indeed you were, but you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God." See here too: with mention of "our God," that is, of the Father, the Holy Spirit sanctifies the faithful of Corinth, with Christ working together. No creature can sanctify another at all; the bestowal of sanctification is the bounty of majesty alone. In this passage, in "the name of Jesus Christ" and "the Spirit of our God," recognize three persons. Second Corinthians: "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all." The grace of Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit plainly express three persons. Also in Second Corinthians: "Now it is God who establishes us with you in Christ, and who has anointed us, and who has sealed us and given the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts." See the unity of the undivided Trinity in its works. The Father establishes and seals us through Christ, and, being about to give himself, he already gives through himself in the present the Holy Spirit as a pledge. In earthly dealings, a down payment is some portion of the contract for which it is given, but the value of a pledge exceeds the worth of the thing for which it is deposited. Here, however, since nothing can be ranked above majesty, its pledge must be equal to it. For what is perfect cannot be surpassed; so the Father grants the pledge of the Holy Spirit in place of himself. Let nothing in the Holy Spirit, then, be thought only half-full, for he is set equal to fullness. For it is not right that he who is given as a pledge in God's stead should be believed to be anything other than God. Also to Titus: "He saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out on us abundantly through Jesus Christ." See here too, plainly within the Trinity, the Father pours out the abundance of the Holy Spirit through the Son, and, what is especially to be noticed, he ascribes the power of regeneration and renewal to the Holy Spirit himself. Peter too, in his letter, sets out the Trinity as inseparable in its persons, saying: "According to the foreknowledge of God the Father, in sanctification of the Spirit, for obedience and sprinkling with the blood of Jesus Christ: may grace and peace be multiplied to you." In foreknowledge the Father is shown, in sanctification the Holy Spirit, in the sprinkling of blood Christ.
XIII. THAT THE HOLY SPIRIT IS NOT BOUNDED BY PLACE.

Let us show from his powers and works that the Holy Spirit is God. Every creature is subject to a beginning in time, and in the same way it knows that it is bound to a place, enclosed within fixed spaces and limits. The Holy Spirit is not confined by any boundaries, as a made thing is. Because of this very freedom of his far-reaching majesty, he must be held to be God. These are the words of the Lord and Saviour to the apostles: "The Father," he says, "will give you the Spirit of truth, to be with you forever." If the Spirit were bound to a place and remained in them forever, he certainly could not be anywhere else. Let us see whether his nature is fixed within local limits. The Lord says to the apostles: "You will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth." After the Lord's ascension the Holy Spirit came upon them, and there appeared to them divided tongues as of fire, and it rested on each one of them.

Let us see why the blessing of different tongues was given first. Surely it was so that the apostles might be made fit to instruct the faithful peoples. The reason we are told that the fire rested on each of them is so that we may understand that the Spirit was not divided among many but remained whole in each, as fire usually does. For a lit fire has this nature, as we know: it gives the use of its light to as many people as look at it and at the tip of its purple flame, and it grants the service of its gift to all of them, yet it remains whole and undiminished. So too the power of the Holy Spirit can be proved to admit no limit, however far it flows out and however richly the grace of God's generosity overflows into great numbers of people. In the same way it suffers no loss. Recognize God from the dignity of his works. The apostles, full of the Holy Spirit, were about to give out the treasures of salvation through the whole world. They carry this heavenly gift about within themselves and pass it on to others by the laying on of hands. The one who receives gains, and the one who gives loses nothing. The Spirit is given whole to believers and is still possessed whole by those who give him. The whole world is filled by his outpouring. He spreads out without being thinned and is scattered abroad without being divided.

On that most holy night of rebirth above all, the same one Spirit is at work in his fullness everywhere: from east to west, from the rising of the sun to its setting, from the north and from the sea. People believe that he is present everywhere when he is called upon, and they feel him in the blessing. Countless multitudes are washed in one baptism and, as the apostle said, are made to drink of one Spirit, and they are reborn into the one embrace of the One who adopts them. And so God says: "In those days I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh." [Note that he said, "I will pour out of my Spirit."] He did not say, "I will pour out my Spirit." That is, he meant: I will give out as much of him as the world can receive. You see that the Spirit goes out from the Father and yet is not separated from the Father. He is sent and not lost, poured out and still kept. And the very fact that we read that he is poured out shows how great his fullness is. At the opening of the sacred volume, the book of Genesis testifies: "And the Spirit of the Lord was moving over the waters." "He was moving," it says, "over the waters." The wording itself seems to give him the abundance of one who fills all things and the high position of one who rules. The prophet also bears the same witness and celebrates this magnificence of his, which no extent of space can contain. He says: "Where shall I go from your Spirit?" That is: Where shall I hide myself from the sight of the one who, I do not doubt, is present everywhere, both within and without? His eye pierces the depths, and I fear it even in the secret places of my heart. I know that everything he has founded lies open to his presence. Because he is a consuming fire, I clearly understand that it was said of him: "There is no one who can hide from his heat." His greatness is beyond words. It enters, fills and goes beyond the depths of the underworld, the expanse of the seas, the breadth of the lands and the heights of the heavens.

He is said to be sent by the Father and the Son and to proceed from their substance, and he is known to do one work with them. That is why the Son says of him: "the Paraclete, who proceeds from the Father." He did not say "who was created by the Father," but "who proceeds from the Father"; that is, the Spirit shares in the Father's power and has the Father's own nature. Moreover, the word itself, when he is said to proceed from the Father, shows that he has no beginning, just as the Father has none. But why is the Son said to be born of God the Father, while the Holy Spirit is said to proceed? If you ask how the one who is born differs from the one who proceeds, the difference is plainly this: the one is born from one, while the other proceeds from both. So the fact that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father shows three privileges of deity in him. It proves that he subsists in his own person, that he endures without any span of time, and that he exists entirely from the Father's substance. So when we are told that he proceeds, the very meaning of the word shows that no laws of time contain him and that he has neither beginning nor end. We read: "I am who I am," and: "He who is has sent me." In the same way, "he proceeds" points to this. For "to be" and "to proceed" both express one and the same eternity. The procession itself, then, has no first point and no last, and so it is understood to be subject to neither beginning nor end.

So we should not believe that he is bound to a place just because we learn from Scripture that the Father sends him. For we also read that the Father and the Son come down and come, as though by a kind of movement. Let us see where. "My Father and I," he says, "will come and make our home with him." And again, when the giants were trying to build a tower up to heaven, the person of the Father speaks: "Come, let us go down and confuse their language." Here, then, the sounds of our own words show our senses how things are brought about. But divine power does not move from place to place. It does not arrive by a course that carries it forward, nor does it leave by a course that slips back. For where can he withdraw to, when he goes beyond all things? Of the Holy Spirit we have learned from sacred Scripture: "And the church had peace throughout all Judea, walking in the fear of God, and was filled with the comfort of the Holy Spirit." In view of this, how can anyone dare to claim that he is a creature bound to a place? He is proved to fill a church of countless people. So it is clear that what the apostle says also belongs to him: "the Father of mercies and the God of all comfort." We have in the psalm: "The rushing of the river gladdens the city of God." What is this rushing river? Surely it is the one the Lord speaks of through John: "Whoever believes in me, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water." The Lord Jesus says this of the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive.

See how magnificent his majesty is. He is given to the church of God on earth in such a way that he still gladdens the city of God in heaven. The city of God means the citizens of the heavenly kingdoms, the peoples of the host above: the principalities, powers and dominions. He waters them with joys beyond words, which spring from their awareness of eternal blessedness. He fills them to overflowing with an abundance of gladness, and with the torrent of his sanctifying power he stirs the choirs of heaven to rejoice. If you think that such great gifts are given through any creature, you leave nothing that belongs to divine power alone. If, I say, you think that these things are given through some creature, you are insulting the angels and archangels, since you suppose that they receive gifts of such greatness and kind from the generosity of a fellow servant.
