II. Whether, as uninformed people suppose, the Holy Spirit became incarnate as the Son did, since he too came upon Mary, or whether only the Son was born of the Virgin.
III. The objection of Macedonius, in which he impiously claims that the Holy Spirit is a more excellent creature.
IV. Macedonius, asserting a duality, denies that the Holy Spirit has his own person.
V. The objection that the saying we read, "Unless one is born again of water and the Spirit," shows that water and the Holy Spirit are equally creatures.
VI. Where it is asked whether the title "Holy Spirit" should be thought of as an epithet or as a name.
VII. That clear testimonies prove that the Holy Spirit fills the prophets in a special way, and that he is both believed to be God and called God.
VIII. Where it is shown that the temple of God is the temple of the Holy Spirit.
IX. Where, against the Novatianists, it is shown that God gave the Gentiles repentance that leads to life, and the very order of the passage shows that this God is the Holy Spirit.
X. Where, in the First Letter to the Corinthians, the Holy Spirit is declared to be God by the way he distributes powers.

XI. It should be noted that the apostle speaks of one Holy Spirit just as he speaks of one God. This could in no way be said of a common creature, nor could it be said that a creature divides gifts to each one as it wills.
XII. Where he says that those who have been made the temple of the Holy Spirit ought to grow so far that they become worthy to carry God in their body.
BOOK TWO
THAT NO RATIONAL CREATURE CAN BE POURED INTO A CREATURE OF ITS OWN KIND.

We read of the abundant outpouring of the Holy Spirit: "And Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan." Who, then, could fill the one who fills all things, unless he himself had the same fullness? The divine word reports of the apostles: "And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke the word of God with boldness." A little later it says: "for the grace of the Holy Spirit had been poured out on the nations." He is said to fill whole nations, yet he is known to remain inexhaustible and full in himself. If the Holy Spirit was created, of what angel or archangel have we ever read that it was received within someone and poured itself into any soul? Tell me if you have ever read of any power or might among creatures that fills and possesses many people at once and, still more, remains undiminished and undivided. It is impossible for a spiritual and rational creature ever to be poured into a nature of its own kind, just as one material thing cannot pass into another material substance. God alone is simple, subtle and pure, and in him the Holy Spirit is also understood. He alone flows into his creation, whether angelic or human, by the power of his bodiless divinity. That divinity alone penetrates its own work and enters the hidden places of the human heart. But no heavenly creature can pour itself into a human being or fill him so far that it can know the hidden things of human thought. That is why we read of God alone: "You alone know the hearts of men"; and again: "For he knows the secrets of the heart." If knowing a person's secrets belongs to divinity alone, how much more is searching the depths of God the mark of supreme majesty in the person of the Holy Spirit!

This privilege belongs only to the Creator: he alone can enter the secret places of the conscience. One soul can be joined to another soul, or one angel to another angel, but neither can be poured into the other. Creatures of this kind can hold only the Holy Spirit, that is, God alone. They are their potter's vessels. They can be filled only by the one who made them from nothing, and without him they feel empty. So the substance of the soul, being in a sense bodily matter, cannot be poured into another rational creature at all. Compared with the grossness of the outer man, the soul can be called bodiless. But in relation to its Creator it is undoubtedly bodily, by the Maker's right. To him its matter can be grasped and his handiwork touched. He can shut it up within a body, bind it, and hand it over to everlasting fire, as we read: "that they may go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels."

But perhaps you will say: "It is obvious that demons often pour themselves with relentless violence into people whom they have been allowed to tempt." That is not so. They can enter the hidden places of the body, but they cannot reach the inner depths of the soul. We must understand, then, that the cunning subtlety of the spirits of wickedness attacks and disturbs those parts of the body that are sometimes worn down by too much wine or by the heat of fever. So hostile temptation knows how to creep into the soul's senses through malice, but by its nature it cannot flow into the soul's inner recesses. That is why human minds and hearts do not take in such unclean spirits because one nature is poured into another. Rather, they conceive them through the corruption of their own wills. So it is clear that demons cannot penetrate the substance of souls, since they cannot know their consciences. If demons do sometimes come to know them, it is because people betray themselves by giving in to them, not because of the power of the demons' nature.

Only divine power, then, which is also in the Holy Spirit, pours itself into rational creatures and surrounds them and mingles with them. In a special way, it rested with overflowing grace in that body of the Lord's humanity, taken from his mother Mary, as the Son of God himself says of himself: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me." Suppose, then, that the Holy Spirit were something made, of subordinate rank, as they say. It would have been as impossible as it was unworthy of God for that creature to fill the soul or body in which the Son of God, that is, God, was already present, and in which, as the apostle says, the whole fullness of the Godhead already dwelt bodily. If the Holy Spirit is a creature, how can corruption possess incorruption, or a frail nature possess what contains the divine majesty? If the Holy Spirit is one of the common crowd of made things, how does a creature dare to share one dwelling in the Saviour's soul with the Creator, that is, with the Son of God, as an equal, a servant with his master? And how does the Creator's servant come to add to the store of holiness, as though the Son were not enough in that soul? It is not so. Rather, the heavenly temple recognizes a fellowship joined to itself. It is no wonder that the Son and the Holy Spirit share one dwelling in that glorious soul of the blessed body, since heaven too is plainly common to them both.
II. WHETHER, AS UNINFORMED PEOPLE SUPPOSE, THE HOLY SPIRIT BECAME INCARNATE AS THE SON DID, SINCE HE TOO CAME UPON MARY, OR WHETHER ONLY THE SON WAS BEGOTTEN OF THE VIRGIN.

But someone says: "If the Holy Spirit dwelt in the Redeemer's body and soul, then the Spirit himself will seem to have taken flesh as well." That is not so. Before that creation began, Mary's sacred body was filled by the Holy Spirit. As the creation began, the Virgin's son was conceived with the Holy Spirit working together with the Son. But it was specifically the person of the Son that was poured into that human being. The Son was to possess him for nine months and to come out with him into the light. The person of the Holy Spirit did not share that time with him in the secret of the virgin's womb. So the Holy Spirit entered the man whom the Son of God took up at the very beginning, but he entered not as the one who took him up but as the one who sanctified him. Within that man the Spirit acted as Christ's partner, while Christ acted as the one who made him his own. For the Son is born; the Spirit is poured in. The soul or flesh of the Virgin's son can be called personally and specifically the soul or flesh of the Son of God, but in no way that of the Holy Spirit. In the humanity in which the Son of God, that is, the Lord of glory, is said to have been crucified, the Holy Spirit can in no way be said to have suffered. So there is a difference of works, not a difference of substances. We cannot say that the Father came down in the form of a dove, or that the Son spoke in the Father's voice when it said, "This is my Son." In the same way, we cannot claim that the Holy Spirit was born of the Virgin, or lived in the Redeemer's flesh in a special way, or was crucified in his passion, or returned to the body in his resurrection, or was raised up to heaven in his ascension. These things must be assigned to the work and person of the Son. It is not fitting to ascribe them to the Holy Spirit, although the unity of their will remains whole.

Meanwhile Macedonius claims that the Holy Spirit is a creature. Let him start wherever he likes, so long as he does not presume to argue from his own words. He must not stray from the track of the sacred law by reasoning that is foreign to the holy pages. If he can, let him bring forward authority from the testimonies of Scripture at every point, enough in number and strength to outweigh the faith of the whole world. Without doubt, great arguments and abundant and very clear proofs are needed for anyone to prove that he is one of the creatures. All the kingdoms of the earth celebrate him as sharing the same honour and glory with the Father and the Son. The catholic church, reborn in him, acknowledges him as her creator. And rightly so: she does not hesitate to believe that the one she sees as her restorer is also her maker.
III. THE OBJECTION OF MACEDONIUS, IN WHICH HE IMPIOUSLY CLAIMS THAT THE HOLY SPIRIT IS A MORE EXCELLENT CREATURE.

"I call him a creature," you say, "but more excellent than all creatures." We said at the beginning that we would build our case not on our own arguments but on the oracles accepted by the catholic church. So, since we are discussing God, let the prophet, the apostle and the evangelist answer us. You call him a creature more excellent than all creatures. Show me in which books you have read these words about the Holy Spirit. You will not show them in the Old Testament, I think, nor in the New. Since you cannot produce them, you confirm our position because you cannot explain your own. By failing to prove that he is a creature, you show that he is the Creator, even without our saying a word. This assertion of yours has nothing to do with the catholic understanding, and nothing at all to do with Christian teaching. So recognize it as an invention of the devil. Whenever he sees the house of the soul empty of the Holy Spirit, he breaks into it as the opposing spirit, together with a dreadful company of sevenfold wickedness. For whoever shuts out the one lets in the other. That "more excellent creature" you speak of was found in the one who shone in heavenly brightness. He was aware of the gift but ignorant of the Giver. He saw what he had but did not know that he had received it. So, swollen with pride, he lost the glory that he had not understood while he was blessed, saying: "I will ascend above the stars of the clouds, I will set my throne above the thrones, and I will be like the Most High." He had no one above him among the creatures, I believe. He saw no one between himself and God whom he might envy and, spurred on by pride, rise up against. And so, seeing no one ranked above him in the heavenly host, he presumed to make himself equal to the Lord of all things himself. If he had found anyone more excellent than himself in the heavenly ranks, he would have been unable to bear a superior, and he would have tried to measure himself against that one, or set himself above that one, instead.

There are two kinds of being in heaven: the one who rules and those who are ruled, the Creator and the creature. No third kind has ever existed between them, greater than the second and lower than the highest. The archangels might perhaps be called more excellent creatures, although they stand above the others more in rank than in nature. But even the archangels serve the Holy Spirit. One of them, as his minister, announced the Spirit's coming to blessed Mary. But you say: "Look, here the prophet Amos clearly calls the Holy Spirit a creature, when he says: 'Behold, I am he who makes the thunder firm and creates the spirit.'" First, the bare word "spirit" can in no way refer to the person of the sanctifying Spirit unless you add "Spirit of God," or "Holy Spirit," or "the Spirit blows where he wills." That is, you must add something that shows the dignity of his work or of his proper name. Next, if you look at the order of the passage, the prophet presented this creature, which you call more excellent, as very lowly indeed, since he described it as created after the thunder. On your reading, then, he would have ranked this chief work of God below an element without reason or feeling, or at least put it on a level with one. That would make no sense. It would be unworthy to believe such a thing of an angel, or indeed of any righteous man.

It seems much nearer to reason and more in keeping with it, then, to understand that after the thunder the prophet means the gusts of the winds. So it says in the psalms: "the winds of the storms that carry out his word"; or: "sulphur and the wind of the storms"; or: "with a violent wind shattering the ships of Tarshish." The word "spirit" can be understood in various ways when it is not specially marked out by its distinguishing titles. But leave these aside and consult the true sense of the Hebrew. There you will find the shameful error of your argument exposed, for there you will find it stated plainly: "For behold, I am he who forms the mountains and creates the wind." See what bare and empty words you have trusted against God! See what a mighty argument you armed yourself with against the power of his majesty! After this, are you not afraid to cling to so weak a twig, when you are hanging over so terrible a cliff?
IV. MACEDONIUS, ASSERTING A DUALITY, DENIES THAT THE HOLY SPIRIT HAS HIS OWN PERSON.

Next you bring in a duality and say that the Holy Spirit has no person of his own. You do not perceive that you have lost the grace of regeneration, you who set out to offend the Regenerator, whom divine truth declares to be united with the Godhead in a communion of majesty and power, saying: "Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." "In the name," it says, "of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." The singular name speaks of unity, while the different designations speak of trinity. In name, then, he is one, but in the distinction of persons he is not one. What is the privilege of one name shared by three, if not the undivided concord of the deity? Set up a scale of rank, if you can, where, as God himself attests, you find nothing but one. You hear three, so that Sabellian impiety may not mingle and confound the unity; you hear one, so that Arian perversity may not divide the Trinity; you hear "Holy Spirit," so that the explicit property of a distinct name may run Macedonius through. Thus the work that is done where the abolition of sins and freedom from guilt are bestowed is not the work of a creature, but the incommunicable work of the Creator. Yet within this inseparable embrace of majesty, in the property of person the Father is one, the Son another, the Holy Spirit another, but in divinity none is anything other; and surely the Spirit, if he were not God, could not have his own person alongside the Father and the Son. Then again, when the Word passes into flesh, and God puts on the condition of man, and "his tabernacle is round about him," and he wraps his splendour in the darkness of our frailty and "makes darkness his hiding place," there is indeed a twofold substance, of God and of man, but there is nevertheless one person. Why? Because when God, taking the form of a servant, is joined to the servant, the lowliness of the lesser is hidden within the reverence due to the greater, and, emptied, it is consumed by the light of the higher; and so the humanity, overshadowed or surpassed by the divinity, does not obtain a property of person. Parity of persons, then, can exist only where there is equality of merits and dignities; and therefore you should know that the Holy Spirit possesses, with the Father and the Son, the one privilege of majesty, since you see that he holds the proper right of a person. But if someone objects and says, "If we speak of two substances in Christ, who is God and man alike, why should we not by the same reasoning believe in two persons?" the answer is that it is not so. For whoever makes two persons in Christ introduces the impiety of a quaternity, which the nature of things utterly refuses to admit. From two rational and different substances, especially those of God and man, of Creator and creature, one substance cannot be made; but from two persons one person can be made, just as we read that the head and the body, Christ and the church, constitute one person: "for the two," it says, "shall be in one flesh." And just as among us humans the son of the head of a household, alongside his father, or the slave alongside his master, does not have the standing of a person in his own right, so in God and man there is indeed a twin substance, but not a twin person; for a person can absorb a person, but a substance cannot absorb a substance, since person is a matter of law, substance a matter of nature.

At this point it seems necessary for us to establish by testimonies that in Christ, God and man alike, there is one person and two substances. Take the one person of God and man in the Redeemer, the person of whom the apostle speaks: "For had they known the wisdom of God, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory." If you ask how the inviolable could suffer and the incomprehensible be crucified, it is the unity of the person that makes us believe that what the man endured, God endured. Likewise, when the evangelist records, "No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven," how does he here assert that the Son of Man, before the passion or the resurrection or the day of the ascension, both descended from heaven and remains in the heavens, unless this is explained by the unity of the person in accordance with the truth? So too in another place the person of head and body is joined together, when we read: "I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me drink." What does the unity of person accomplish here? The man is fed and God is refreshed; the foot is warmed and the head testifies that it feels the warmth. So he says, "they would never have crucified the Lord of glory," and conversely, "No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven." See how, because of the unity of the person, human things are mingled with divine and divine things with human. God is crucified, and the man is said to descend from heaven and to remain in heaven.

Since this is so, let us examine from the sacred books the distinction of the twofold substance. Blessed Moses says: "You shall eat the head with the feet, and you shall devour its entrails." Let us take the feet to mean the humanity and the head the majesty. So it comes about that when, with searching faith, we recognize these things hidden within the letter, we consume the entrails of the lamb, that is, the hidden things of the mysteries. For the greed to devour is understood as zeal for searching. So also in another place the same revealer of mysteries hints at the explanation of the twofold substance, saying: "Foxes have holes and the birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head." That is: deceitful heresies and the dark or aerial powers have established their seat in human hearts with deep-rooted dominion, but the hearts of unbelievers, seeing me as a man in the flesh, do not believe that I am God hidden within the man. For holes and nests signify not passing and momentary dwellings but ones founded in lasting and secure possession, which multiply the serpentine nourishment of vices. The apostle too has set out the two substances plainly, with the obscurity of mystery removed, saying: "Our fathers, from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever."

But you say: the apostle, in the volume of his works, confesses only two persons, as when he says to the Corinthians, "Paul, called to be an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God," and to the Galatians, "Paul, an apostle not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead," and again, "one God the Father, from whom are all things and we in him, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him." On this basis you say that no mention is made of the Holy Spirit. To put it briefly, you have forgotten that the apostle, full of the Holy Spirit, preached these things about the Father and the Son to the peoples by the Spirit's own inspiration. So when he spoke of the working of the Father and the Son, the one who dictated what he was to say was not absent, according to the saying, "And no one says 'Lord Jesus' except in the Holy Spirit." You see, then, that whoever is to believe in Christ, or confess him, or preach him, must first have the Holy Spirit within him. So do not let it weigh on your faith that the Father and the Son are sometimes mentioned without any mention of the Holy Spirit. For often, with the Father's name left unspoken, the working of the Son and the Holy Spirit is proclaimed. Holy Ananias says to Paul: "Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus, who appeared to you on the road by which you came, has sent me so that you may see and be filled with the Holy Spirit." Here there is plainly a connection of two persons. See: Paul is rebuked by Christ by being blinded, and is filled by the Holy Spirit by being enlightened, and no mention of the Father is included here.

Likewise, when Paul asked certain disciples, "Into what were you baptized?"—disciples who, it was established, had been baptized with John's baptism after the Lord's ascension, after the baptism of the Trinity had been proclaimed; and even that mystery by which John had been accustomed to baptize, namely into him who was to come, was shown to have been left out of their baptism, as the apostle Paul says to them, "John indeed baptized, but into him who was to come," which is to say, "You were not baptized in this way"—when Paul asked them, "Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?" (the Spirit whom those duly baptized after the Saviour's baptism certainly ought to have confessed through the laying on of hands), they answered, "We have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit." When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus, and when Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied. Notice that when they are baptized in the name of Jesus, they afterwards receive the Holy Spirit and prophetic power through the invocation of the Paraclete. Truly he is God who, after the gift of God, adds increase to fullness.

See, with two persons named in the baptism, we do not read that the Father was invoked; yet, as we must believe, he works together with the Son and the Holy Spirit in unity of power and deity. The sacred reading was silent about his presence; it did not deny it. So when the Holy Spirit had come upon them, then they spoke in tongues and prophesied. See how great the power of the Holy Spirit is. In baptism the forgiveness of sins is granted; at the coming of the Holy Spirit the gifts of powers are conferred, and miraculous signs are performed by those who have been confirmed. Those who are strangers to the truth are in the habit of quibbling even over syllables. For although we know that it was said without qualification of the Trinity, "For from him and through him and in him are all things," they assert that "from him" means more than "through him," and likewise that the preposition "through" carries a greater privilege than "in him." But if they think that "in him" is said of the Holy Spirit as implying lesser power, let them hear how magnificent this preposition is, and accept that, even by their own assertion, it must be understood of the Holy Spirit: "In him," it says, "we live and move and have our being." And rightly do we live and move and have our being in him, in whom we have been restored and regenerated. But we know that "through him" is also to be referred to the Holy Spirit, as you have it: "To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge"; likewise in Hebrews: "who through the Holy Spirit offered himself without blemish to God"; and again: "The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us." And even if we understand "from him" of the Father, we quite often find "from" said of the Holy Spirit as well, as we have in John's Gospel: "What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit," and at the end of the passage: "So it is," it says, "with everyone who is born of the Spirit."

So it is no disparagement of the Holy Spirit when the works of the Father and the Son are recorded and his name is left unspoken, just as the Father and the Son are not denied when a work or power of the Holy Spirit in particular is affirmed, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles: "You will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now," and as the Gospel also says about the single person of the Holy Spirit: "Unless one is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God." Shall we believe that in this passage the Father and the Son were absent from so great and so divine a gift because they are not named? Not at all. For without doubt they are joined in the mysteries and benefits with the Holy Spirit, with whom they share one substance, and they are present, if not by being mentioned, then by the unity of their goodness and work.
V. THE OBJECTION THAT THE SAYING WE READ, "UNLESS ONE IS REBORN OF WATER AND THE HOLY SPIRIT," SHOWS THAT WATER AND THE HOLY SPIRIT ALIKE ARE CREATURES.

But you say: the Holy Spirit is so much a creature that he appears joined to the element of water, which is placed here first in position and order, according to the Gospel saying cited above: "Unless one is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God." It is plain that whoever says this is ignorant not only of the divine power in the Holy Spirit but of the very meaning of baptism. For the apostle says: "If we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with Christ." If you ask how we can die or rise with Christ, pay attention. All of us who are plunged into the sacred font imitate the death and burial of the Redeemer, as the same apostle says: "Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized in Christ have been baptized into his death? For we were buried with Christ through baptism into death." For just as he was laid in the tomb by a three-day death, so we too, placed by a threefold immersion within the water, that is, within the bosom of a fellow creature, are buried as we go down and raised as we come up. Through the water, then, the imitation of burial is carried out; through the Holy Spirit the reality of life and the hope of eternal salvation are conferred. Indeed, take away the invocation of the Holy Spirit, and let us see whether the mere pouring of that water can do any good at all. So it is a creature that imitates the office of burial; it is God who grants the benefit of rebirth. Recognize that the one whom you perceive to be the parent of our restoration is also the author of our resurrection. Of him the prophet foretells, speaking thus to the Father: "Send forth your Spirit and they shall be created, and you will renew the face of the earth." What is the difference between the working of the water and that of the Holy Spirit? Through the water we are seen to be led down into the tomb; through the Holy Spirit we are shown to be made ready for the kingdom.
VI. WHERE IT IS ASKED WHETHER THE DESIGNATION "HOLY SPIRIT" SHOULD BE CONSIDERED A SURNAME OR A NAME.

But meanwhile you think it must be asked whether the designation of the Holy Spirit, who must also be called God, is a name or perhaps a surname. But recognize that what we usually add to a name among men is not fitting for the majesty of God, in whose name nothing whatever is added on, but everything is without doubt everlasting by nature. Even the teaching of grammar calls some nouns common, that is, appellative, and others special, that is, proper. Let us see whether we can find something similar here in our own subject. Take the special or proper names in God, namely Father and Son and Holy Spirit. These are so proper that Father cannot be said of the Son, nor do we readily read Holy Spirit said of the Father. Take likewise as proper: unbegotten, begotten, proceeding from both. Again, take the general and common names: majesty, immensity, fullness, one, the only God. But when you hear "one," no counting begins here; rather, an infinite perfection is summed up. What is "one" but an incommunicable name, which admits neither a later nor an earlier? What is "one" but a simple, uncompounded and undivided substance? What is "one" but the unchangeable and equal and ever the same, who can never differ from himself? And so the common designation speaks of unity, the proper designation of trinity. So when you say Father, Son, Holy Spirit, you have set out the persons of each one individually; when you say one God, you have shown the common substance of the Trinity, its common glory. Here, then, ignorance has drawn the night of error over itself, when it suppresses the term of majesty and judges the Holy Spirit only by the name that, as we have said, is proper to him, rather than by the one he shares with the Father and the Son.
VII. THAT THE HOLY SPIRIT IN A SPECIAL WAY FILLS THE PROPHETS, AND IS LIKEWISE BELIEVED TO BE AND CALLED GOD, IS PROVED BY CLEAR TESTIMONIES.

Scripture reports that the Holy Spirit in particular spoke through Moses and David and Isaiah and the other prophets, yet divine [?] declares that it was God who spoke, as we often find in the book of the Pentateuch: "The Lord spoke to Moses, saying." So let us ask more carefully whether it is specifically the Holy Spirit who speaks in the prophets. As we said before, we have in the Acts of the Apostles the words of Paul when he was rebuking the Jews: "The Holy Spirit spoke well through Isaiah to our fathers: 'Hearing you will hear, and you will not understand.'" In the same book we read: "Men and brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled which the Holy Spirit foretold through the mouth of David." And in the letter of Peter we read: "For prophecy was never brought by human will, but holy men of God spoke by the Holy Spirit." Let us recognize that the grace of prophecy plainly belongs to the power of the Holy Spirit. And concerning a psalm of David we read in Hebrews: "Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says: 'Today, if you hear his voice'" and so on. Here too he testifies most plainly that the Holy Spirit spoke through David.

Now let us see whether the one by whom all prophecy is said to have been inspired is God. Luke asserts that it is the Lord God who spoke through the prophets, saying: "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and brought about the redemption of his people," and he added: "as he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets, who have been from of old." Thus the oracle of the Gospel proclaims outright that the Holy Spirit, who had inspired the prophets, is the Lord and God of Israel. In what follows, Simeon, filled with the Holy Spirit, "had received a revelation from the Holy Spirit," it says, "that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord's Christ." When he saw him and took him in his arms, he blessed God, that is, the one from whom he was seen to have received the revelation. He blessed God and said: "Now, Lord, you let your servant depart in peace." See how he calls the Holy Spirit outright Lord and God, the Spirit by whose word and revelation he had learned that he would see Christ. You see, then, that these prophetic sayings are to be understood specifically of the Holy Spirit: "The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken," and: "I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me." Know that this name, "Lord God," is to be referred here to the person of the Holy Spirit, who spoke in David. Or at least recognize in the one God the will of the three, the power of the three and the substance of the three. For when you say "Father," the person of one is understood, but when you say "God," the whole Trinity is meant.

We also learn in the Acts of the Apostles that it was undoubtedly God who had foretold the sufferings of Christ through the prophets. For it says: "But God, who foretold through the mouth of all the prophets that his Christ would suffer, has thus fulfilled it." "His Christ" means the one filled with the gift of his anointing. And again: "which God spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets from of old." When it says, "which God spoke through the mouth of his holy ones," it says "his holy ones" because sanctification belongs properly to the Holy Spirit. We read in Isaiah: "Do I not fill heaven and earth, says the Lord?" Who is this Lord who says through Isaiah that he fills heaven and earth, if not the Holy Spirit, who filled Isaiah himself with prophetic power and the spirit of truth? Just as the will of the Trinity assigns the prophetic dispensation to the Holy Spirit, so it also assigns to him, above all, the grace of the second birth. As he says in John: "What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit." In another place the power of renewing man is written to lie with the Holy Spirit: "But you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now." And, as was said above: "Unless someone is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit." And to Titus: "He saved us," it says, "through the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit." Let us see who this is whose children we become by the grace of adoption: "He gave them," it says, "power to become children of God," and again: "who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God."

You see most plainly that this Holy Spirit, in whom we are reborn, is God, and that his fatherhood is given to us as a gift. In another place he himself declares this more clearly than daylight: "I will be a father to them, and they shall be my sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty." He is rightly called Almighty, for he blots out the record of sin, loosens the chains of conscience, strips the one who believes in him of the foulness of a corrupted nature, adorns him with the garment of innocence, the beauty of righteousness and the robe of immortality, and in his loving fatherhood transfers his children into the state of the angels. Let no one think that the Holy Spirit should be classed among creatures. One who can grant eternal freedom stands outside the condition of slavery. For the apostle says: "You did not receive a spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as children, and the Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God." He who makes us children of God through the forgiveness of sins is undoubtedly God.

It is agreed that the whole creation, even that of the angels and archangels, was liable to sin. Yet the fall of those who transgressed established the obedience, care and love of the rest toward God. It became a confirmation of their humility, submission and steadfastness, and a recognition of their frailty. Unless the Holy Spirit were free above all things, he could not make free men out of slaves. For if he were a creature, however much God bestowed on him the grace of holiness, he would still have remained conscious of being a debtor. That is why it says: "No one can forgive sins but God alone." Whoever this opponent is, let him choose which he prefers: either let him confess that the Holy Spirit, who forgives sins, is God in every respect, or, if he does not believe that pardon for sins can be granted through him, he has emptied out for himself the benefit of regeneration and the sacrament of baptism. It belongs to God alone, then, to loose what is bound, to restore what is corrupted, and to cleanse what is stained. Therefore, aware of our weakness and of his majesty, we cry out to him with groaning: "Against you alone have I sinned." That is: you alone are not bound by the law of sin; you alone are a stranger to it, not by your conduct but by your nature; and so you alone can release debtors, since you alone are free from debts. What you have you did not borrow from elsewhere; you are full from what is your own. For no one gave to you first, nor are you watered by powers drawn from somewhere else, nor has anything been poured into you from another. You yourself are the source of your river and of your glory. Yours is a nature which, just as it knows no beginning, so it has received nothing from anything before it.
8. Where it is shown that the temple of God is the temple of the Holy Spirit.

The sacred Scriptures define the Holy Spirit as the one who properly dwells in the human heart: "The Father," it says, "will give you another Paraclete, to remain with you forever." And to the Corinthians: "He will give life also to your mortal bodies through his Spirit, who dwells in you." So we rightly understand this text to have been written about the Holy Spirit: "The kingdom of God is within you." Those who are found worthy to prepare themselves as his temple are surely God's kingdom: God's temple, and not a creature's. Listen to the voice of the one who dwells in us, speaking through the apostle: "You are the temple of the living God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you." And in another place: "As God says: 'I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God.'" See: the very one who dwells in the temple of the human heart declares that he is God. Ananias was among those who honored God by selling the property they had gained by honest labor and laying the proceeds at the apostles' feet. He is known to have made a vow to God, and he is accused of lying to the Holy Spirit, as the apostle Peter says: "Ananias, why has Satan tempted your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit?" And he went on to add: "You have not lied to men but to God." What does this mean? He sins against the Creator. Does Scripture then make his sin smaller, so that, as the impious would have it, it declares him guilty toward a creature and makes him a debtor to a lesser being for an insult to a greater one? Not so. The one against whom the offense of sacrilege is committed is plainly endowed with divine power. Of him it says in another place: "But whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will have no forgiveness, either in this age or in the age to come." So when Ananias tempted God by his transgression, he is said to have deceived the Holy Spirit. Recognize, therefore, that the Holy Spirit and God share one cause, one glory and one reverence. That is why Peter concluded about the Holy Spirit most clearly in the words that follow: "You have not lied to men but to God."

While Peter was speaking to Cornelius, the circumcised believers who had come with Peter were astonished that the grace of the Holy Spirit had been poured out on the Gentiles as well. You see that the Holy Spirit bestowed grace not from what belonged to another but from what was his own. If you ask who it is that gave this grace, Peter goes on to teach it, saying: "If, then, God gave them the same grace." Earlier he plainly declared this giver of grace to be the Holy Spirit, and here he declares him to be God. There by his proper name, here by the common name, the same confession is shown to be repeated. When he says, "the grace of the Holy Spirit has been poured out on the Gentiles as well," the one who is the author of grace is God by nature. It belongs to God alone to bestow the gifts of grace from what is his own, so that the apostle can be seen to have spoken of him when he said: "I labored more abundantly than all of them, yet not I, but the grace of God with me." He who dispenses grace and human salvation is rightly declared to be God. And Peter adds: "Who was I that I could hinder God?" He meant surely that God who poured himself out on the Gentiles, or on Cornelius, in a flood of overflowing grace.
9. Where, against the Novatianists, God gave the Gentiles repentance unto life; and the very order of the passage shows that this God is the Holy Spirit.

Notice how, with regard to the person of the Holy Spirit, who suddenly filled Cornelius and his companions, the name of God is celebrated with many testimonies: "When they heard this," it says, "they fell silent and glorified God, saying: 'So God has given repentance unto life to the Gentiles as well.'" Here, against the Novatianists, we must note that God is said to give repentance, which he surely bestows in no other way than through the ministry of his servants. So when Peter says, "Who was I that I could hinder God?" and again, "So God has given repentance unto life to the Gentiles," what interpretation need we wait for in matters so plain? Whom, whether ignorant or unbelieving, would this confession of the divine name, repeated so often at the coming of the Holy Spirit, fail to satisfy?
10. Where, in First Corinthians, the Holy Spirit is declared to be God by the distributions of powers.

Hear from Corinthians a text that alone could be enough to establish the divinity of the Holy Spirit. He says in the Letter to the Hebrews: "God bearing witness with signs and wonders and various powers, and by distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his own will." Let us ask the apostle himself whether this distributor of gifts is one of the creatures. We have in First Corinthians: "I make known to you that no one speaking in the Spirit of God says 'Jesus is accursed,' and no one can say 'Jesus is Lord' except in the Holy Spirit." Notice how he has here declared in the most absolute terms that the Spirit of God is the Holy Spirit. Concerning the Holy Spirit, whom in the previous sentence he presented as speaking as the Spirit of God, look at what follows and see how plainly it testifies that he is God and Lord: "There are varieties of gifts," he says, "but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of workings, but the same God." It is as if the blessed apostle had been consulted about the divinity of the Holy Spirit. Of the one of whom he had said "the same Spirit," he plainly adds: "the same God, who works all things in all." He could not work all things if he were one among all things. Recognize that here the Holy Spirit, as much under his own name as under the names "Lord" and "God," is either clearly expressed or at least joined to the Trinity. But in the distribution of gifts the divine word is understood rather to have meant the Holy Spirit, since we learned above that the grace of distribution belongs to the Holy Spirit by a special dispensation. And as for his words "the same Lord" and "the same God," he shows in the following passage that they are to be referred to the Holy Spirit, when he says: "To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another the gift of healings in the one Spirit, to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the discerning of spirits, to another various kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of speech. But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each as he wills." He is subject to no one; he is the Lord of heaven, who bestows heavenly gifts by his own will and by the right of his own power.

11. It should be noted that, just as he speaks of one God, so he speaks of one Holy Spirit, which could in no way be said of a common creature; nor could it be said of such a creature that he distributes to each as he wills.

You see that, just as there is one Father and one Son, so there is also one Holy Spirit, as he goes on to state: "For we have all been given to drink of one Spirit." If the Spirit belonged to the common mass or multitude of creatures, he could not be called "one" at all. And since you have here the words "to another is given faith in the same Spirit," the same apostle has declared to the Corinthians who it is that grants this faith, saying: "and to each as God has apportioned the measure of faith." You see that he declares without any doubt that this apportioner of faith is God. In so rich an outpouring of such great gifts, the very magnificence of the work speaks for itself of the power of its author. Yet he concluded about him this way: "But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each as he wills"; as also in another place: "The Spirit breathes where he wills"; and again: "and by distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his own will." Here, then, there is no service of subject slavery but the free choice of authority, and in the distribution of heavenly goods there is the inexhaustible kindness of supreme generosity. As for the words "and by distributions of the Holy Spirit," he taught the Corinthians whether this distributor, that is, this apportioner, is God, saying: "and there are varieties of workings, but the same God." We read in the Acts of the Apostles: "Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you bishops to rule the church of God." The chosen vessel declares to the Corinthians that the one who appointed bishops in the church is God, saying: "God has appointed some in the church." What God is this, if not the Holy Spirit? The distribution of graces shows that this is the office of his person, as follows directly in the same passage: "God has appointed in the church," it says, "first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then powers, then gifts of healing, helps, governments, kinds of tongues." "God has appointed some in the church," it says. That he said "God" here of the Holy Spirit is made clear by the very dispensation of sanctifications and powers, which belongs to the Holy Spirit. For it is he who enriches the mouths of the prophets, dispenses the remedies of healing and multiplies the adornments of grace. When he flowed into the apostles, the miracles of signs and the various kinds of tongues proclaimed that he is the God of the universe.
12. Where he says that those who have been made the temple of the Holy Spirit ought to advance so far as to be worthy to carry God in their body.

So the apostle says to the Corinthians: "Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit?" Earlier passages of the same letter clearly show that the temple of the Holy Spirit is the temple of God, when they say: "Do you not know that you are the temple of God and the Holy Spirit dwells in you?" "And the Holy Spirit," it says, "dwells in you." Who could doubt that they are the temple of that God whose dwelling place they are shown to be? And after saying, "Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit?" he concluded the passage with brilliant truth: "Glorify and carry God in your body." So whoever prepares in his heart a temple of earnest purity for the Holy Spirit carries God in his body through chastity and the mortification of the flesh. We must carry bodily the one by whom we are spiritually possessed. Therefore know that the one you see is worthy of a temple must be adored with divine honors, celebrated with prayers and worshiped with sacrifices. So the teacher of the Gentiles says to the universal Church: "Do you not know that you are the temple of God and the Holy Spirit dwells in you?" This is possible for no creature. It is the mark of the divine majesty to fill whole peoples one by one, each individually, and yet to remain in the immensity of its own fullness. It is, I say, a unique and proper attribute of the divine nature to be present in every place, to enter into all things and to contain all things. It belongs, I say, to God alone to strip the children of perdition of the debts of their nature, to renew them with cleansed consciences, to make them children of God and to raise them up into the glory of the heavenly kingdom.
